lead: A compensator is an extra block placed with the plant so the closed-loop system meets its specification. Root-locus design moves the dominant closed-loop poles to a chosen point; Bode design shapes gain crossover, phase margin and gain margin. Both routes can produce a lead block, which adds phase, or a lag block, which adds low-frequency gain. They are used in servo drives, power converters and process loops where a plain gain cannot meet both speed and steady-state error. Some syllabi call this analytical design of controllers.
prereq: You need: Unit 3 root locus and Unit 4 Bode plots and margins; chapter 5.4 to 5.6 for the compensator forms.

blocks.text: Specifications come first. A specification may give damping ratio ζ, natural frequency ω<sub>n</sub>, settling time, steady-state error, or margins. Convert time-domain targets to a desired dominant pair s<sub>0</sub> = −ζω<sub>n</sub> ± jω<sub>n</sub>√(1−ζ²). The uncompensated locus usually misses s<sub>0</sub>; the compensator bends it through s<sub>0</sub>.

Root locus uses the angle criterion. For s<sub>0</sub> on the compensated locus, ∠C(s<sub>0</sub>)G(s<sub>0</sub>) = ±(2k+1)180°. The magnitude criterion then sets gain: |C(s<sub>0</sub>)G(s<sub>0</sub>)| = 1. If the angle is short by φ, a lead zero and pole supply that φ. A lag pair placed near the origin supplies gain without much angle change at s<sub>0</sub>.

Bode uses the open-loop frequency response L(jω)=C(jω)G(jω). Gain crossover ω<sub>gc</sub> is where |L|=1, that is 0 dB. Phase margin PM = 180° + ∠L(jω<sub>gc</sub>). Gain margin GM = −20 log<sub>10</sub>|L(jω<sub>pc</sub>)|, where ω<sub>pc</sub> is the phase crossover. Lead raises PM near crossover; lag raises low-frequency gain for smaller steady-state error.
The two routes share the same C(s), so a design from one route must be checked by the other.

blocks.where: s<sub>0</sub> is the desired closed-loop pole; C is the compensator; G is the plant; k is an integer; the angle is in degrees.

blocks.text: Draw the uncompensated root locus and mark s<sub>0</sub>. Compute the angle deficiency φ = ±(2k+1)180° − ∠G(s<sub>0</sub>). This is the phase the compensator must add at s<sub>0</sub>.

For a lead, use C(s)=K<sub>c</sub>(s+z)/(s+p) with |p|>|z|. Its angle at s<sub>0</sub> is ∠(s<sub>0</sub>+z) − ∠(s<sub>0</sub>+p). Choose z and p so this equals φ. Place the zero near a slow plant pole and the pole farther left. Then K<sub>c</sub> = 1/[|(s<sub>0</sub>+z)/(s<sub>0</sub>+p)| |G(s<sub>0</sub>)|].

For a lag, use |z|>|p|. Put the pole close to the origin and the zero to its left. The angle at s<sub>0</sub> is small, while the gain ratio z/p raises the error constant. Keep the lag pair well below the expected crossover.

After choosing C(s), find all closed-loop poles. Check that no extra pole is closer to the imaginary axis than s<sub>0</sub>. If one is, the response is dominated by that pole and s<sub>0</sub> is not useful.
Plot the uncompensated G(jω). Read its PM, GM and low-frequency gain. Decide the new gain crossover from the required PM plus a safety margin of about 5°.

For lead, place the zero below the new crossover and the pole above it. The maximum phase occurs at ω<sub>m</sub> = √(zp), and the peak phase is sin φ<sub>m</sub> = (p−z)/(p+z). Set ω<sub>m</sub> near the new crossover. The lead raises PM and bandwidth, so the response is faster but more noise-sensitive.

For lag, place the zero and pole below crossover. The pole is closer to the origin than the zero, so the low-frequency gain rises by z/p. Keep the lag phase at crossover small, usually a few degrees. The cost is lower bandwidth and a slower response.

Verify both routes. A root-locus point check does not give PM or GM. A Bode margin check does not place the dominant poles. Use a step response, percent overshoot, settling time, steady-state error, PM and GM. If one check fails, adjust the compensator and repeat.

figure.caption: A specification feeds two parallel design routes, root locus and Bode plot, which both lead to a lead or lag compensator and then verification. In the worked example, C(s)=16(s+2)/(s+4) gives L(s)=16/[s(s+4)], ωgc=3.14 rad/s and PM=51.8°.

spec.aria: A specification feeds two parallel design routes, root locus and Bode plot, which both lead to a lead or lag compensator and then verification.

examples.question: For G(s)=1/[s(s+2)] with unity feedback, a lead C(s)=16(s+2)/(s+4) is proposed. (a) Check that s<sub>0</sub>=−2+j2√3 is on the compensated root locus. (b) Find the gain crossover frequency and phase margin of the compensated open loop.
steps: Compensated open loop: C(s)G(s) = 16(s+2)/(s+4) × 1/[s(s+2)] = 16/[s(s+4)]. The plant pole at −2 cancels with the compensator zero at −2; this is allowed here because the cancelled pole is stable.
At s<sub>0</sub>=−2+j2√3, the vector s<sub>0</sub> has angle 120° and magnitude 4. The vector s<sub>0</sub>+4=2+j2√3 has angle 60° and magnitude 4.
Angle of L(s<sub>0</sub>) = 0° − 120° − 60° = −180°. This meets the angle criterion, so s<sub>0</sub> is on the compensated root locus.
Magnitude at s<sub>0</sub>: |L(s<sub>0</sub>)| = 16/(4×4)=1. The magnitude criterion holds with the built-in gain 16.
For frequency response, L(jω)=16/[jω(jω+4)]. Set |L(jω)|=1: 16/[ω√(ω²+16)]=1, so 256=ω²(ω²+16).
examples.answer: The point s<sub>0</sub> = −2 + j2√3 lies on the compensated locus; the gain crossover is 3.14 rad/s and the phase margin is 51.8°.
examples.check:
import math
w = math.sqrt((-16 + math.sqrt(1280))/2)
pm = 180 - (90 + math.degrees(math.atan(w/4)))
print(round(w, 2))
print(round(pm, 1))

traps: Cancelling a plant pole in C(s)G(s) can hide an unstable or lightly damped mode; check the cancellation and internal stability.
Meeting a root-locus point does not guarantee PM or GM; meeting Bode margins does not guarantee the desired dominant poles.
Lead increases bandwidth and can amplify noise; lag reduces high-frequency gain but adds phase lag, so keep its corner below crossover.
Do not confuse gain crossover with phase crossover: PM uses gain crossover, GM uses phase crossover.
Do not mix degrees and radians in phase calculations; atan in code returns radians unless you convert.

quiz.q: State the angle criterion for a point s<sub>0</sub> to lie on the root locus of 1 + K G(s)H(s)=0.
quiz.a: ∠G(s<sub>0</sub>)H(s<sub>0</sub>) = ±(2k+1)180°, k integer, with magnitude 1 for the chosen K.

quiz.q: Why does a lag compensator reduce steady-state error without much change to phase margin?
quiz.a: It raises low-frequency gain by the ratio z/p > 1, lowering steady-state error; its pole and zero are placed well below gain crossover, so their phase lag at crossover is small.

quiz.q: A lead compensator adds 25° at crossover. The uncompensated PM is 30°. Estimate the new PM, ignoring other changes.
For L(jω)=16/[jω(jω+4)], find the gain crossover frequency.
quiz.a: Set 16/(ω√(ω²+16))=1. Square: ω⁴+16ω²−256=0. Take x=ω²: x²+16x−256=0, x=9.889, so ω=3.14 rad/s.

quiz.q: A root-locus design places s<sub>0</sub> correctly but the Bode PM is 12°. Explain what went wrong and what to do.
quiz.a: The design ignored other poles or a near cancellation; PM measures the frequency response, not just one point. Check all closed-loop poles, add lead phase or move the zeros and poles, then verify the time response.

quiz.q: Why can a Bode-designed lag compensator slow the response?
quiz.a: Lag reduces high-frequency gain and adds phase lag. If crossover moves to a lower frequency, bandwidth falls, so rise and settling time increase. The zero and pole must be placed well below crossover.

GM = −20 log<sub>10</sub>|L(jω<sub>pc</sub>)| in dB, where ω<sub>pc</sub> is the phase crossover frequency where ∠L(jω<sub>pc</sub>)=−180°. Positive GM means the gain can increase by that factor before instability.

quiz.q: What is the difference between gain crossover and phase crossover?
quiz.a: Gain crossover is where |L|=1, that is 0 dB; phase margin is measured there. Phase crossover is where ∠L=−180°; gain margin is measured there.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, compensator design is often done with CAD tools that sweep parameters and check robustness. Loop shaping uses the same Bode ideas, while state-space pole placement generalizes the root-locus aim. Digital implementation adds sampling delay, so margins shrink in practice. Search for loop shaping, sensitivity function and H-infinity design if you want the modern version.
